title: Twisted Tea Hangover: Why Malt Drinks Hit So Hard
excerpt: Why Twisted Tea, Mike's Hard Lemonade, and Four Loko leave you wrecked: big cans, hidden ABV, sweetness that speeds drinking, and how to count drinks and recover.
metaDescription: Why Twisted Tea, Mike's, and Four Loko hangovers hit hard: big cans, hidden ABV, and sweet taste. How to count drinks, prevent it, and recover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Twisted Tea, Mike's Hard Lemonade, Four Loko, and other flavored malt beverages don't contain a special hangover ingredient. They give people rough mornings mostly because they're easy to drink fast, they come in big cans, and some versions are much stronger than they taste. A 24-ounce can of a 5% hard tea is about two standard drinks. A 23.5-ounce can of Four Loko at 12% to 14% alcohol is roughly four to five. Add sugar that hides the taste of alcohol, carbonation that can speed absorption, and the habit of treating these drinks like soda, and a "few cans" can quietly turn into a night of heavy drinking.

**The quick rules:** Count drinks by alcohol, not by cans. Check the ABV on every can, because "Extreme," "Harder," and "Max" versions can be 8% or more. Sip a glass of water between cans, eat a real meal first, and treat a single Four Loko as a full night's worth of drinking, not a starter. Never mix these drinks with energy drinks or pre-workout, because caffeine can hide how drunk you are.

> **This is general information, not medical advice.** Most hangovers from flavored malt beverages pass within a day. **Get help right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or long pauses), has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, and the person should not be left alone to "sleep it off." **See a doctor soon if** you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, you have severe stomach pain, you see blood in vomit, your heart is racing or pounding for hours, or you feel far worse than any hangover you've had. If you have diabetes, take medicines that interact with alcohol, or are pregnant, talk to your doctor about whether these drinks are safe for you.

## What Is a Flavored Malt Beverage, Anyway?

A flavored malt beverage, often shortened to FMB and sometimes called an "alcopop," is technically closer to beer than to a cocktail. In the United States, the base is brewed from malted grain, like beer. Makers then filter much of the beer color and flavor out to leave a fairly neutral alcoholic base, and add flavors, sweeteners, colors, and sometimes tea or juice. Federal rules set by the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) require most of the alcohol in these products to come from that malt base rather than from added spirits, which is why they're taxed and sold like beer and show up in grocery and convenience stores.

That's the category that includes:

- **Hard teas**, such as Twisted Tea, which is brewed with real tea and flavored to taste like sweet iced tea.
- **Hard lemonades and fruit drinks**, such as Mike's Hard Lemonade and its stronger "Harder" line.
- **High-strength "supersized" cans**, such as Four Loko, which is sold in tall single cans with a much higher ABV than regular beer.
- **Some hard seltzers**, which are often made from a fermented sugar or malt base. Seltzers are usually lower in sugar, so we cover them separately in our [hard seltzer hangover guide](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

The point to take from this is simple: chemically, the alcohol in a Twisted Tea is the same ethanol that's in beer, wine, or vodka. What's different is everything around it, and that's where the hangover story really lives.

## Why Does Twisted Tea Give Me Such a Bad Hangover?

This is the most common question people search, and it usually has a boring but useful answer. Twisted Tea Original is around 5% alcohol, about the same as a regular beer. On paper it shouldn't be any worse. But in practice, a few things push people toward a heavier night than they planned.

### It tastes like sweet tea, not alcohol

The whole design of a hard tea is to taste like something you'd drink at a barbecue. The sweetness and tea flavor cover the bitterness and burn of alcohol, so there's no natural "slow down" signal from your taste buds. People who would nurse a beer for 20 minutes can finish a can of hard tea in half that time. Drinking speed matters a lot, because the faster alcohol goes in, the higher your blood alcohol level climbs, and peak levels are closely tied to how bad you feel the next day.

### The cans are bigger than they look

Twisted Tea is widely sold in 24-ounce single cans and in large party formats, alongside the standard 12-ounce can. A 24-ounce can at 5% contains about 1.2 ounces of pure alcohol. In the US, one standard drink is 0.6 ounces (14 grams) of pure alcohol. So one tall can is two drinks, and three of them is six drinks, which is well into what the CDC defines as binge drinking for both men (five or more drinks on an occasion) and women (four or more).

### The stronger versions are easy to grab by mistake

Twisted Tea Extreme and similar "extra" versions are around 8% alcohol. A 24-ounce can at 8% is a little over three standard drinks. Because the flavor is nearly the same, it's easy to drink a stronger can at the same pace as a regular one.

### Sugar, then a crash

Regular hard teas are sweet. The exact amount varies by flavor and size, so check the label, but a standard 12-ounce can of the original flavor carries a couple dozen grams of carbohydrates, much of it sugar. There's no good evidence that sugar on its own causes hangovers. What sugar does do is make the drink easier to keep drinking, and for some people a lot of sugar plus a lot of alcohol leads to a shaky, low-energy feeling as blood sugar swings the next morning. Alcohol also interferes with the liver's ability to release stored sugar, which is one reason people wake up weak and craving carbs.

### Some caffeine from the tea

Because it's made with tea, Twisted Tea can contain a small amount of caffeine. It's much less than a cup of coffee and much less than an energy drink, so it's unlikely to be the main problem. But if you're drinking several tall cans late at night, even a little caffeine on top of alcohol can make sleep lighter, and poor sleep is a big part of why hangovers feel so draining.

## Is Twisted Tea Worse Than Beer for a Hangover?

Drink for drink, probably not by much. A 12-ounce Twisted Tea at 5% and a 12-ounce beer at 5% contain the same amount of alcohol, and the amount of alcohol you drink is the single biggest predictor of hangover severity in the research we have. The Alcohol Hangover Research Group, an international team that has studied hangovers for years, consistently finds that how much people drink and how high their blood alcohol gets matter far more than the type of drink.

Where hard tea can be worse in practice:

- **Pace.** It goes down faster than most beers.
- **Serving size.** Tall cans make it easy to underestimate how many drinks you've had.
- **Sugar.** Beer has carbohydrates too, but very little of it tastes sweet. Hard tea's sweetness keeps you sipping.

Where beer can be worse: some darker or heavily hopped beers carry more of the by-products of fermentation called congeners, which are covered below. If you want a deeper look at how beer itself affects the morning after, see our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover).

## Mike's Hard Lemonade Hangover: What's Different?

Mike's Hard Lemonade follows the same pattern. The original is around 5% alcohol, and the "Mike's Harder" line is stronger, commonly around 8% in tall cans. It's sweet, tart, and very easy to drink cold on a hot day, which is exactly when people tend to drink more and drink faster.

A few things people notice with hard lemonades in particular:

- **The citrus acidity.** Lemon-flavored drinks are acidic, and alcohol already irritates the stomach lining. If you're prone to heartburn or an upset stomach after drinking, several cans of a sour, sweet, carbonated drink on an empty stomach is a likely recipe for a queasy morning. Our [heartburn after drinking guide](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains why this happens and what helps.
- **The sweetness.** Hard lemonades are among the sweeter malt drinks, so the "doesn't taste like alcohol" problem is strong here.
- **Summer conditions.** Day drinking in the sun means you're sweating while alcohol is also making you pee more. That's a fast way to feel dried out by evening, and our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) walks through what's actually going on.

The fix is the same as for hard tea: know which version you're holding, count drinks by alcohol, and put a glass of water between each can.

## Four Loko Hangover: Why It Hits So Hard

Four Loko deserves its own section, because it's in a different league from a regular hard tea or lemonade.

### One can is several drinks

Four Loko is commonly sold in 23.5-ounce cans at 12% to 14% alcohol, depending on the product and the state's rules. At 12%, a can holds about 2.8 ounces of pure alcohol, which is close to five standard drinks. At 14%, it's more than five. In other words, one can contains about as much alcohol as four or five regular beers, and two cans is a heavy night by any measure.

That's why people who say "I only had one Four Loko" so often wake up feeling like they had a lot more. They did.

### It used to contain caffeine, and the habit of mixing remains

Four Loko became notorious around 2010, when the original version combined high alcohol with caffeine and other stimulants. In November 2010, the US Food and Drug Administration sent warning letters to several makers of caffeinated alcoholic beverages, saying added caffeine in alcohol was an unsafe food additive, and the products were reformulated without added caffeine.

Today's Four Loko doesn't have added caffeine, but many people still mix it, or similar drinks, with energy drinks. That's a bad idea. Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol level or make you less impaired. It mainly makes you feel more alert, which can lead to drinking more than you otherwise would and staying up later, both of which make the next day worse. We cover this in detail in our guide to [energy drinks and alcohol](/never-hungover/energy-drinks-and-alcohol).

### Why it can be dangerous, not just unpleasant

Because so much alcohol is packed into one sweet, fizzy can, it's possible to reach a dangerous blood alcohol level faster than people expect, especially if they drink quickly, haven't eaten, or are smaller or less used to alcohol. If someone who has been drinking high-strength cans is confused, can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy, or is breathing slowly, treat it as an emergency and call 911. Our guide to [blackout drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains why memory loss is a sign you drank too fast, not a normal part of a night out.

## Malt Beverage Hangover vs Liquor, Wine, and Seltzer

People often wonder whether a "malt liquor" style of drink is inherently worse than a vodka soda or a glass of wine. Here's how the main factors compare.

### Congeners

Congeners are by-products of fermentation and aging, such as methanol, certain alcohols, and other compounds that give drinks some of their flavor and color. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues, published in 2010 in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, found that people reported somewhat worse hangovers after high-congener bourbon than after low-congener vodka at the same amount of alcohol. The difference was real but modest compared with the effect of the alcohol itself.

Flavored malt beverages are filtered, light-colored, and not aged, so there's no strong reason to think they're high in congeners. Direct studies on Twisted Tea, Mike's, or Four Loko and hangover severity aren't available, so it's fair to say congeners probably aren't the main story here. For more on this, see our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### Carbonation

There's some evidence that bubbles can speed alcohol absorption. A small study by Roberts and Robinson, published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2007, found that many participants reached higher blood alcohol levels faster with carbonated vodka than with flat vodka. Not everyone responded the same way, and it was a small study. Still, it fits with what many people notice: fizzy drinks seem to "hit" faster. Most malt beverages are carbonated, as are beer, seltzer, and champagne.

### Sugar and sweeteners

Compared with a plain hard seltzer, most flavored malt beverages are much sweeter. Compared with a cocktail made with juice or soda, they can be similar. There's no good evidence that sugar itself causes a hangover, but sweet drinks are easier to drink quickly, and that's the indirect path. If you're curious about how mixers stack up, our guide to the [best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) goes through common options.

### Artificial colors and flavors

Some of these drinks, especially the bright fruit flavors, contain added colors and flavorings. People sometimes blame the dye for their headache. There's no good evidence that food dyes cause hangovers, and the amount of alcohol is a far more likely explanation. If you notice a specific drink always gives you a headache even in small amounts, it's reasonable to avoid it, but don't let a dye theory distract from counting drinks.

### The bottom line on drink type

If two people drink the same amount of alcohol at the same pace, the type of drink makes a modest difference at most. Flavored malt beverages earn their bad reputation mostly through how they're packaged and how they're drunk: big cans, high ABV versions, sweet taste, and fast sipping.

## How to Count Your Drinks

This is the most useful skill for avoiding a bad morning after any malt beverage. You can work out standard drinks in a can with a simple rule:

**Ounces in the can × ABV (as a decimal) ÷ 0.6 = standard drinks.**

Some quick examples:

- 12 oz at 5% (regular Twisted Tea or Mike's): 12 × 0.05 ÷ 0.6 = **1 drink**
- 24 oz at 5% (tall can of regular hard tea): **2 drinks**
- 24 oz at 8% (tall can of an "Extreme" or "Harder" version): **about 3.2 drinks**
- 23.5 oz at 12% (Four Loko): **about 4.7 drinks**
- 23.5 oz at 14% (stronger Four Loko): **about 5.5 drinks**

Most people's liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies with body size, sex, genetics, food, and medications. Nothing speeds that up: not coffee, not a cold shower, and not a big glass of water. So two tall cans of an 8% drink is more than six hours of work for your liver, even if you finished them in 45 minutes.

## How to Prevent a Malt Beverage Hangover

None of these steps guarantees a hangover-free morning, but together they make a real difference for most social drinkers.

1. **Read the can before you open it.** Check both the size and the ABV. If it says Extreme, Harder, Max, or anything above 6%, treat it as more than one drink.
2. **Decide your number in drinks, not cans.** "Three drinks" might mean three 12-ounce cans, or just one and a half tall cans.
3. **Eat a real meal first.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. A meal with protein, fat, and carbs works better than a bag of chips.
4. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between every can slows your pace and helps with the fluid loss alcohol causes.
5. **Pour it into a glass with ice.** It sounds small, but it slows you down compared with drinking straight from a tall can, and it lets you see how much you're actually drinking.
6. **Skip the energy drink mix.** Don't combine these drinks with energy drinks, pre-workout, or caffeine pills.
7. **Stop a couple of hours before bed.** Alcohol close to bedtime cuts into deep sleep. Stopping earlier and drinking some water before bed gives your body a head start.
8. **Watch the summer combo.** Heat, sun, and sweet cold drinks are a classic setup for drinking more and getting dried out. Keep water nearby and take shade breaks.

For a broader plan that works for any kind of drink, see our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## What to Do the Morning After

If you already overdid it on hard tea, hard lemonade, or a Four Loko, here's what tends to help most:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water or an electrolyte drink through the morning rather than chugging a liter at once, which can upset a queasy stomach.
- **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, rice, or soup can help settle your stomach and steady your blood sugar after a sugary night.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one, take a single label dose with food and water. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol both affect the liver, and ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the safe way to think about this.
- **Rest.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, so a nap or an early night helps more than most remedies.
- **Don't drink more to feel better.** "Hair of the dog" just delays the hangover and adds more alcohol for your body to clear.

Most hangovers ease within 24 hours. If you're still very unwell after that, or you have any of the warning signs listed at the top of this page, get medical advice.

## Who Should Be Extra Careful With These Drinks

- **People new to drinking or with lower tolerance.** The sweet taste and big cans make it easy to drink more than you can handle, quickly.
- **Smaller people.** The same can produces a higher blood alcohol level in a smaller body.
- **People with diabetes.** Sweet malt drinks can raise blood sugar at first, while alcohol can cause low blood sugar later, especially overnight. Talk to your doctor about how to drink safely, if at all.
- **People on medications.** Many common medicines, including some antidepressants, sleep aids, allergy medicines, and blood thinners, interact with alcohol. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.
- **People with acid reflux or sensitive stomachs.** Sweet, acidic, carbonated drinks can make heartburn and nausea worse.
- **Anyone under 21 in the US.** These drinks are marketed with bright colors and candy-like flavors, but they are alcoholic drinks, and high-strength cans can be dangerous for inexperienced drinkers.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who enjoy a few hard teas at a cookout use dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, as part of their routine. Research on DHM is promising but early. Much of it comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest DHM may support how the body processes alcohol and may help protect liver cells, and human data is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents a hangover if you drink a lot, and it doesn't lower your blood alcohol level or make it safe to drive. It is not a substitute for counting your drinks.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it and when. If you take prescription medicines, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Twisted Tea, Mike's Hard Lemonade, and Four Loko don't have a secret hangover chemical. Their alcohol is the same ethanol as in any other drink. What makes them rough is that they taste like soda or iced tea, come in big cans, and in some versions pack two to five standard drinks into a single serving. Count your drinks by alcohol, check the ABV on every can, eat first, alternate with water, and never mix them with energy drinks. Treat a Four Loko as a whole evening's drinking. And if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, or is vomiting while drowsy, don't wait it out: call 911.

For the bigger picture, our [ranking of drinks by hangover risk](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) puts every major drink type side by side, and our guide to [congeners](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains the by-products behind the differences. Our [beer vs liquor hangover](/never-hungover/beer-vs-liquor-hangover) comparison covers where malt drinks fit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does Twisted Tea give me a hangover?**

Mostly because of how much alcohol it's easy to drink. Twisted Tea Original is about 5% alcohol, similar to beer, but it tastes like sweet iced tea, so people drink it faster. It's often sold in 24-ounce cans that hold two standard drinks each, and stronger versions like Twisted Tea Extreme are around 8%. The sugar and a small amount of caffeine from the tea may play a minor role, but the total alcohol is the main cause.

**Is Twisted Tea worse than beer for a hangover?**

Drink for drink, not by much. A 12-ounce Twisted Tea and a 12-ounce beer at the same ABV contain the same amount of alcohol, and research consistently shows the amount of alcohol matters far more than the type of drink. Hard tea tends to be worse in practice because its sweetness makes it easy to drink faster and lose count, especially with tall cans.

**How many beers is one Four Loko?**

A 23.5-ounce Four Loko at 12% alcohol contains about 4.7 standard drinks, roughly the same as four or five regular 12-ounce beers. At 14%, it's more than five. That's why a single can can lead to a heavy hangover, and why two cans is a lot of alcohol for anyone.

**Does Mike's Hard Lemonade give you a worse hangover?**

Regular Mike's is about 5% alcohol, like beer, so the alcohol per can is similar. The stronger "Harder" line is around 8% in larger cans and can contain three or more drinks per can. Its sweetness, tartness, and carbonation make it easy to drink quickly, and the acidity can upset the stomach for people prone to heartburn. Counting drinks by alcohol and alternating with water helps most.

**Does the sugar in malt beverages cause hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that sugar on its own causes a hangover. The bigger issue is indirect: sweetness hides the taste of alcohol, so people drink more and faster. Large amounts of sugar and alcohol together can also leave some people feeling shaky and low on energy the next day as blood sugar swings.

**Are flavored malt beverages beer or liquor?**

In the US, they're legally closer to beer. They're brewed from a malt base, filtered to remove most beer flavor, and then flavored and sweetened. Federal rules require most of the alcohol to come from the malt base, which is why they're sold where beer is sold. The alcohol itself is the same ethanol found in any drink.

**Is it safe to mix Four Loko or Twisted Tea with energy drinks?**

It's not a good idea. Caffeine doesn't make you less drunk, but it can make you feel more alert, which often leads to drinking more and staying up later. The FDA warned makers of caffeinated alcoholic drinks in 2010 that added caffeine in alcohol was unsafe, and those products were reformulated. Mixing them yourself brings back the same problem.

**Can DHM help with a Twisted Tea hangover?**

DHM is a plant compound with promising but early research, mostly from animal and lab studies, suggesting it may support alcohol metabolism and liver health. There is no good evidence that it prevents a hangover after heavy drinking, and it doesn't lower blood alcohol. If you try it, use it alongside counting drinks, eating, and drinking water, not instead of them.
